title: Hello [Open] World: Unbody Is Now OSS (Alpha)
author: amir
blurb: Unbody is releasing its AI-native backend as open source (Alpha), offering a modular, Supabase-style stack designed for building transparent and trustworthy intelligent systems.

summary.summary: This is the first modular backend for the AI-native era built together in the open.
Unbody is a data knowledge driven, AI-native backend designed to replace traditional stacks.
The system is architected for modularity, autonomous agent support, and plugin extensibility.
We are building the Supabase of the AI era and inviting you to help shape it.
You can find the project at github.com/unbody-io/unbody.
When we launched Unbody commercially, it was an experiment powered by curiosity and frustration.
It became clear that we could not build an excellent product without involving the wider developer community.
We are releasing Unbody as open source to build a better product and gain developer adoption.
By opening Unbody, we are taking our first step toward building transparent AI infrastructure that prioritizes user control.
This alpha release focuses on architectural flexibility and modularity rather than feature completeness.
The modular design supports both traditional plugins and autonomous AI agents.
The Contextual Data Engine transforms raw data into structured and interconnected knowledge.
The architecture supports integrations with tools like Unstructured.io and LlamaIndex.
The open-source version already outclasses our cloud service in terms of architectural openness.
Our cloud offering includes production-grade features but comes with locked-in storage and inflexible pipelines.
The open-source version allows you to choose your own storage solutions and AI models.
Our content API remains unchanged despite significant refactors in data ingestion and processing.
Our roadmap envisions the eventual replacement of our cloud version with this open-source powerhouse.
We are sharing Unbody OSS Alpha to open a discussion with the wider community.
The AI tooling ecosystem is scattered, requiring developers to make dozens of complex decisions.
We asked what if there were a Supabase, but for the AI era.
Supabase simplified building modern web apps by offering a unified, developer-friendly stack.
Unbody aims to bring that spirit to AI-native software that reasons, adapts, and acts.
Supabase is great, but it wasn't built for a world where your backend needs to think.
Traditional stacks store static data in tables, but AI-native products demand a different approach.
This is because the way we interact with software has fundamentally changed.
We now talk to software and expect it to reason and take action on our behalf.
Backend software must evolve from storing static data to managing dynamic, enriched knowledge.
AI-native software relies on knowledge that is enriched, connected, and semantically aware.
Software needs a dynamic, evolving graph of meaning to mimic human intelligence.
Processes like vectorization and summarization should be essential infrastructure, not extras.
A backend must process images, video, and audio to build software that understands like a human.
Unbody is a Supabase-style stack for building AI-native products from the ground up.
Without Unbody, even building a simple Q&A bot requires complex setup steps.
You typically have to spin up a vector database like Weaviate or Pinecone.
Developers must create a pipeline for chunking and ingesting content.
You are left stitching all this into your backend and maintaining it.
Unbody is built for opinionated flexibility, allowing you to bring your own vector store or AI provider.
This image illustrates the Unbody modular stack architecture.
Please see the README on our Github repo for a complete list of modules and plugins.
A backend powering intelligent software needs to work like a brain.
Unbody is built on four functional layers that mirror how intelligent systems operate.
Perception handles how the system sees and understands the world through knowledge fabrication.
Memory manages storage and persistent memory regarding what the system knows.
Reasoning handles how the system thinks, decides, and plans.
Action handles how the system interacts with others via APIs and MCP.
Perception is where raw data becomes structured, enriched knowledge.
Data ingestion connects and pulls content from third-party platforms, local files, or databases.
Processing automatically parses and structures raw multi-modal data from various file types.
Enhancement transforms raw data using pluggable agents like OCR and web crawlers.
Vectorization generates semantic vector representations using models or custom solutions.
Memory is where your enriched knowledge lives, ready for retrieval.
Vector Storage holds embeddings in supported databases like Weaviate or Pinecone.
File Storage persists raw and processed files using local or cloud storage.
Media Serving allows access to media through Unbody’s CDN.
The Metadata Store keeps track of content structure, relationships, and context.
Reasoning is where generation, decision-making, and function execution happen.
Text Generation supports hosted APIs or self-hosted models like GPT-4.
JSON Generation produces structured responses and machine-readable payloads.
Image Generation support for cloud-only visual generation is on the roadmap.
The Function Registry defines callable functions via schema-based definitions.
Execution and Routing dynamically executes functions with intent parsing and argument validation.
Action is where your backend connects to the outside world via APIs and SDKs.
The Content API allows querying your knowledge-base via GraphQL.
The Push API allows you to push structured data directly into Unbody.
The Admin API is used to configure schemas, projects, and permissions.
The MCP connects Unbody to external systems and workflows.
SDKs are available in TypeScript, iOS, and Android.
The system includes chat endpoints with memory and long-term context.
We offer integration with observability monitoring systems.
We are in feedback mode and want to know what works and what needs improvement.
We are releasing the alpha to build with community feedback and invite you to try it.
You can find our GitHub Repo at the link provided.

title: The End of the Container Era: Apps Are a Historical Glitch
author: amir
blurb: The friction of modern digital work, characterized by open tabs and siloed tools, is not natural but a symptom of the 'Container Era.' This essay argues that apps are a historical glitch and explores a future architecture built around human intent rather than rigid software boxes.

summary.summary: We accept the fatigue and scattered attention of modern work because we lack a name for it.
This friction is actually a symptom of a specific architectural failure.
We mistakenly assume that apps and websites are natural laws rather than mutable constructs.
Software containers are a historical glitch that emerged from past constraints on building and shipping.
Distribution hurdles forced software to be packaged into standalone units like floppy disks or domains.
Technological limits required vendors to ship one static, top-down interface to millions of users.
Software became a fixed shape handed down to us, forcing us to hop between rigid boxes.
The resulting system acts upon three anti-human pillars.
Unlike the physical world, the digital world forces you to travel to the tool.
You are forced to go to specific containers like Gmail or Salesforce to perform actions.
These walled gardens do not talk to each other, making you visit disconnected rooms repeatedly.
This physical separation creates a deeper cognitive fracture.
Previous research reveals we are still trapped in the Page Era.
The Page is a centralized model where content and UI are defined top-down by the server.
Humans explore chunk-by-chunk along threads, rather than thinking in Pages or Apps.
The OS forces you to translate your intent into its rigid language because it doesn't understand your threads.
An image visualizes the disconnect between server-shipped pages and thread-based thinking.
The caption notes that while servers ship Pages, the mind follows Threads.
Tabs are the ultimate symptom of the OS failing to understand the thread of your work.
We pay a price because the logic is siloed and the abstraction is wrong.
You act as a human router, manually copying context from one box to another all day.
The result is a quiet insanity involving dozens of tabs and infinite micro-searches.
You pay this tax with your attention, time, and nervous system.
The dam is breaking as the energy shifts within the builder community.
Innovators like Naval and AGI are proving the future is about pure intent, not navigating menus.
Teams like Zo and Wabi are exploring personal software that fits the user rather than the masses.
We are realizing the use of software is the bottleneck, not the build.
We must rethink the architecture so the app doesn't need to exist at all.
This is part one of a series that will introduce the Faceless Data Layer.
We are cooking up something in stealth that tackles this exact problem.
It feels like the dam is finally breaking as energy shifts in the builder community.
Naval Ravikant and AGI Inc are showing that UI is pre-AI and the future is intent-based.
Projects from Zo and Wabi AI are unbundling environments to create personal intelligent computers.
We are circling the truth that the use of software is the bottleneck, not the build.
A social media link extends the discussion on this topic.
We need to go deeper than just agents and rethink the architecture so the app disappears.
This series will continue by discussing why Agents are just a transition step.
We are working on a stealth project that addresses this architectural shift.

title: "AI-native" v.s. "AI-forced"
author: amir
blurb: Explore the critical distinction between 'AI-forced' tools that fragment development and true 'AI-native' applications that unify product and AI stacks. This post details how Unbody leverages Weaviate to bridge the gap and shift software from providing information to delivering answers.

summary.summary: The shift toward AI-native applications represents a fundamental change where AI becomes the foundation of software rather than just an added feature.
Current AI tools often feel "AI-forced" rather than truly AI-native, creating a development gap despite rapid advancements in machine learning.
The image illustrates the problem of AI-forced development.
Existing tools impose a fragmented toolchain that is neither accessible nor compatible with traditional product development.
The image shows the fragmented toolchain of AI-forced development in practice.
Dual systems for product data and embeddings lead to data sync headaches and redundant management.
Separate API layers for product and AI functions mean double the endpoints to create, maintain, and secure.
Different ETL pipelines for product data versus AI embeddings add unnecessary workflow complexity.
Duplicated cache setups for product data and model responses increase infrastructure load and maintenance.
Distinct CDNs for product assets vs. AI models drive up costs and deployment complexity.
Splitting logs between product and AI metrics creates gaps in monitoring and obscures the complete performance picture.
Different access requirements for product features versus AI models create friction and a heavier security load.
Handling model inference errors separately from regular product errors adds an extra layer of exception management.
Product and model deployments require separate pipelines, complicating releases and increasing coordination work.
Product changes and AI experiments need separate tracking setups, making rollbacks and updates twice as complicated.
Dual backup systems for product data and AI embeddings add storage overhead and complicate recovery.
Separate infrastructure needs for product CPU and model GPU make scaling expensive and add management overhead.
The real barrier to AI-native applications is the sheer duplication and disconnect in tooling that developers currently face.

title: Managing the UI state for generative data flow
author: amir
blurb: Moving beyond CRUD thinking is essential for building effective Generative AI interfaces. This post explores why generative data flows require a shift in mental model towards streaming, multi-stage pipelines, and context-as-state.

summary.summary: While wiring up a demo RAG layer, the UI behavior felt incompatible with the standard fetch/response flow.
The root problem wasn't the code but the mental model of thinking like CRUD developers.
This post explains the conceptual foundation of UI state management for generative flows.
Before managing generative data, we need to strictly define it.
Generative data is output produced on the fly by a model rather than fetched from a static store.
We will use Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) as the main example to keep the discussion grounded.
It helps to contrast generative patterns with the CRUD model we already understand.
Visual comparison of Generative data versus CRUD data structure.
RAG combines user questions with relevant data sources to generate a context-aware response.
Visual diagram showing the RAG flow: retrieve, generate, and respond.
The first step is to retrieve relevant content such as documents or records from your data.
The second step is to generate an answer using that retrieved content as context.
This setup grounds generation in real, retrievable context rather than just training data.
This retrieval-generation flow will be used as the working example for the post.
In CRUD flows, data is a complete fact that arrives when requested.
In generative flows, the response is a real-time interpretation streamed over multiple chunks.
Generative flows lead to three fundamental differences in how we need to think about state.
A CRUD request is typically atomic, consisting of one request and one response.
Visual illustration of the atomic nature of a CRUD request.
RAG workflows are multi-step processes with at least retrieval and generation stages.
Diagram of a minimal multi-stage pipeline showing retrieval followed by generation.
A realistic setup is often more complex than the minimal case.
Diagram illustrating a realistic multi-stage generative pipeline with additional steps.
Since stages fail independently, a single loading flag is insufficient for UI state.
Unlike atomic CRUD payloads, generative flows stream data token by token over time.
Streaming occurs in various models, from sequential text to image refinement distributions.
Failing to think in partial state and streaming updates leads to poor UI experiences.
Visual comparison between atomic parcel delivery and streaming token-by-token output.
A simplified example demonstrates how generative output is typically handled in code.
You don't get data all at once; you build it incrementally as it arrives.
In CRUD flows, fetched data is a precise and complete fact.
Visual contrast between CRUD returning facts and generative systems returning interpretations.
Generative responses are interpretations shaped by inputs, context, and probabilistic models.
The same question can yield different outputs in tone or structure even with identical input data.
While a CRUD response is the truth, a generative response is merely a version of the truth.
This distinction changes how predictable the output is and how the UI handles it.
State management must adapt to data that is multi-stage, streamed, and interpretive.
Generative endpoints return a readable stream of text tokens rather than a single payload.
We must append tokens to the UI as they arrive instead of setting a final result.
Since tokens cost money, the UI must support canceling the stream immediately.
Diagram showing streaming architecture with append and cancel support.
Without mechanism to cancel, you will burn tokens unnecessarily.
Without append logic, you cannot reflect progress accurately in the UI.
Context is the real state you need to manage in generative systems.
The UI reacts to a multi-stage pipeline, and the composition of those stages is the context.
Treat the context as a first-class application state object, similar to a Redux store.
An example of a structured context object in a RAG system.
Visual representation of context structure including prompts, retrieval, and history.
Discarding retrieved records and history discards what made the output possible.
Dropping context essentially throws away the trace of your reasoning.
The context object is the actual state of your generative UI.
Frontend components should bind to the context to persist what the model saw.
This context serves as the truth for regeneration and future editing flows.
Context acts as a contract stating that the response is an interpretation of specific inputs.
The system presents the output as the best interpretation given the current context.
Persisting context makes it easier to explain why a model generated a specific response.
Modeling generation as a pipeline shifts how state is structured in the UI.
Generative flows involve multiple steps, requiring more than simple loading flags.
Your app needs to treat each stage of the pipeline as its own state machine.
Using union types guarantees that the system is never in conflicting states.
State machines allow for precise feedback, such as distinguishing retrieving from generating.
You can retry specific parts of the flow, like generation, without restarting everything.
Switching on state makes UI logic significantly easier to manage.
In generative flows, retries are a feature rather than just error handling.
Users may want a second version or the model might fail to produce valid output.
Because stages are separate, retries should be stage-aware.
Visual diagram of a stage-aware retry flow in generative pipelines.
Managing UI state requires keeping track of context and the pipeline shape.
These principles apply to RAG, OpenAI functions, and LLM tool chaining.
We may release a follow-up post focused purely on the engineering mechanics.
We encourage feedback from those building generative features and infrastructure.

title: From Query to Context: Building Agentic RAG with Unbody's JSON Endpoint
author: amir
blurb: A naive approach to RAG often isn’t enough when handling nuanced user queries like excluding ingredients or setting time constraints. Learn how to build an Agentic RAG pipeline using Unbody’s generative JSON endpoint to parse complex requests into structured search parameters.

summary.summary: I recently spoke at AI Thinkers Abu Dhabi about building robust RAG systems where naive approaches often fail on nuanced queries.
This example query asks for an Italian dish for two people, without sausage, and ready in under 30 minutes.
Agentic RAG parses the query into structured parameters like 'no sausage' to engage in more precise retrieval.
Let’s see how to do this with Unbody step by step.
First, you need a Unbody project set up with your data already ingested and indexed.
Second, you need your API key and Project ID from the Unbody dashboard.
If you haven’t set this up yet, check out the Unbody docs for a quick start.
That’s it, now you can start calling Unbody’s APIs to search, filter, and generate.
Before writing code, knowing your data schema helps determine which parameters to extract from a user’s query.
Knowing available fields in the schema lets us decide which parts of the user’s query should be parsed.
For example, a user might want an Italian dish with no sausage and ready in under 30 minutes.
We know to extract the concept, ingredients to exclude, and a time constraint from this request.
RAG consists of Retrieval and Generation, where retrieval gathers context for the model.
One approach is to take the user’s entire query directly.
You then feed the top documents into a text-generation prompt.
The system doesn’t actually understand the user’s intention and just tries to match the entire text semantic way.
Alternatively, you can parse the user’s query into structured parameters.
You then apply filters to our knowledge base such as excluding sausage or limiting time.
Finally, you generate the final response using only the truly relevant documents.
The general syntax we will be using is going to be with Unbdoy’s chain syntax methods.
To translate this into a proper RAG query, we need to extract three pieces of information.
First, extract main keywords or concepts from the user's query to apply to semantic search.
Second, identifying any specific filters to pass to the where function.
Third, determining the prompt or task description for the generation step.
To do this, we will be using Unbody’s generative JSON endpoint which utilizes the Zod library.
Unbody’s generative JSON receives two arguments: a set of messages with role definition and a zod schema.
In Zod schema we can define what the shape of generative json should be, starting with the concepts field.
We’re expecting an array of strings or null if nothing is extracted.
The describe method adds a note so that the model understands this field represents main search terms.
Next, we need to capture ingredients that the user wants to include using the same method.
The description clarifies that this field is for ingredients the user explicitly wants in the recipe.
Now, let’s expand our schema by adding all the fields we expect from the query.
We add includeCuisineTypes to capture preferred cuisine types.
We add totalTimeMinutesMax to capture a maximum time constraint.
Here’s the full Zod schema with descriptions for every field to guide the extraction.
Now that our schema is complete, lets create a function called queryParser and integrate the entire logic.
We pass our complete querySchema to the generative endpoint.
The system message instructs the model to analyze the query.
The returned payload gives us a well-structured object containing all the extracted parameters.
In this snippet, the model processes the user’s input and returns a structured JSON object.
Now that we’ve parsed the query into detailed parameters, it’s time to build the final RAG pipeline.
We want to search based on the main concepts extracted, falling back to the full query if needed.
This snippet ensures that our semantic search is as focused as possible by prioritizing specific keywords.
Now comes the slightly more complex part: turning each extracted filter into a proper 'where' clause.
If the query has an includeIngredients array, we want to add a corresponding filter.
But we only want to add this filter when includeIngredients actually exists.
We conditionally spread the filter into our query only if includeIngredients exists.
Next, if the query specifies ingredients to exclude, we want to add a filter for each item.
Each ingredient that should be excluded is mapped into a NotEqual filter conditionally.
We are combining all filters using the And operator.
Finally, we combine all these filters into a single query.
This final combined filter checks each parameter and only adds a condition if that parameter exists.
We are generating the final answer with generate.fromMany().
After we’ve retrieved and filtered our documents, we use the generation step to produce a final answer.
The system message instructs the model to consider the retrieved results when generating the response.
This section covers bringing it all together into the complete RAG pipeline.
Here’s what the full API handler might look like in a Next.js project.
The user’s free-form query is processed by parseQuery() which returns a structured object.
Semantic Search focuses primarily on the extracted concepts.
Filtering applies each filter conditionally using the And operator.
Limiting keeps our result set manageable via autocut.
Finally, the fromMany method produces a coherent answer that integrates the retrieved documents.

title: What the F**k is an AI-native app?
author: amir
blurb: Explore why "AI-first" is becoming the new "mobile-first" and discover the three main pillars that define a truly AI-native application.

summary.summary: This post explores the characteristics of AI-native apps and what it means to be AI-first.
The shift in user mentality towards conversing with machines necessitates a corresponding shift to an AI-first software design.
An AI-native app is defined as more human software that understands us and can adapt to human needs.
The first step towards more human-like software is its ability to adapt and tailor to our individual needs and contexts.
A chatbot at work needs to understand your company and team context to effectively search documents or summarize reports.
In the digital world, software needs to access and understand the data footprints we produce daily to provide a personalized experience.
Traditionally, CMS platforms required extensive manual effort to create and manage structured data for apps.
Traditional vs AI-native data management for personalization
Conventionally, existing content like FAQs or docs had to be re-curated manually to fit structured data requirements.
AI-native applications use language models to adapt data in its original format, bypassing the need for manual restructuring.
This process requires the capability to aggregate and process data from all different locations and platforms.
Every piece of content inherently possesses context linked to other data points, unlike isolated traditional content.
Context awareness through semantically connected data sources
Making connections between different islands of information constitutes context, which is a critical element for AI-native applications.
Semantic search allows for a deeper understanding and linking of content beyond simple keyword matching.
Users now expect to communicate with apps through conversation rather than just clicking through options.
Shift from information seeking to conversational interaction with software
There is a growing preference for using natural human language when interacting with software.
To support this interactive approach, we need to implement features like generative search, image captioning, and chatbots.
Technical breakdown of AI-native app components
We break down the essential tech for AI-first apps into data aggregation, data processing, and functions.
Data Aggregation involves getting data from different places and making sure it syncs up nicely.
Data Processing turns raw data into enhanced AI-ready data through tasks like cleaning, chunking, and vectorizing.
The functions division borrows from RAG but goes beyond it to avoid getting too technical.
Data Retrieval acts as a supercharged search engine inside your app to find exactly what you need quickly.
Data Augmentation improves existing data by adding details to help the app understand scenarios better.
Data Generation goes beyond retrieval to create new content on the spot based on what users ask for.

Complexity of assembling a full AI-native system from scratch
Building the system requires Python familiarity and components range from document parsers to deploying LLMs via API.
Real-world apps also require non-AI elements like CDNs, video hosting, and image processing.
